title: Three Miserable Husbands, One Bored God. Save the Tigers Season 3 Drags Marriage All the Way to Heaven.
excerpt: The Telugu marital comedy that owned the group chat is back on JioHotstar — and this time Vennela Kishore plays Lord Indra, looks down at Earth, and decides every married man is walking on thorns.
body:
It begins, as all great Telugu comedies do, with three frustrated men in a bar. **Rahul** is stuck in a job he loathes. **Vikram** cannot move past his divorce. **Ghanta Ravi** has uprooted his family to a new community and is still, somehow, exhausted by all of it. They gather to do what husbands in this universe have always done — complain, beautifully, about the institution of marriage. And then, in the cheekiest narrative swing the franchise has taken yet, somebody upstairs starts listening.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=wob0NDMQqGY</youtube>

**Save the Tigers Season 3** is now streaming on **JioHotstar**, premiering June 19 in multiple languages — and for the Telugu diaspora that has quietly made this one of the platform's most reliable comfort-watches, the timing could not be better. After two seasons of earthbound marital chaos, the show does something delightfully unhinged: it goes celestial.

Enter **Vennela Kishore** as **Lord Indra**, ruler of the heavens, who peers down from his cosmic perch and arrives at a startling cosmic audit — every husband on Earth appears to be deeply, comprehensively unhappy. Aided by his divine sidekicks, Indra observes the struggles of married men and, in the show's signature register, compares marital life to walking barefoot across thorns. Vennela Kishore in a crown, theologically baffled by domestic misery, is exactly the kind of casting that makes you press play before the trailer even finishes.

> "A ROAR that made two worlds collide. Call it God's plan or pure destiny… the TIGERS are back." — JioHotstar's Season 3 promo

The premise from there is pure wish-fulfilment with a sting in the tail. Determined to give the trio a fresh start, Indra dispatches **Chitragupta** — the celestial accountant of human deeds, played by Gundu Sudarshan — to Earth with a life-changing proposal. The three friends wake up in dramatically upgraded lives: one becomes an MLA, another a screenwriter, the third a corporate CEO. The question the season chews on is the one every midnight overthinker eventually reaches — does success, fame and a rewritten life actually change anything about love? Or do the same people just bring the same problems to a nicer house?

The ensemble that made this franchise sing is back. **Priyadarshi Pulikonda** returns as Ghanta Ravi and remains the show's beating heart, that rare comic actor who can land a punchline and a lump-in-the-throat in the same scene. **Abhinav Gomatam** as Rahul brings his impeccable timing, and **Chaitanya Krishna** anchors Vikram's wounded-divorcee arc. The wives — Pavani Gangireddy, Jordar Sujatha and Deviyani Sharma — are not props here; the series has always been smart enough to give them their own ground to stand on, and Vikram's storyline this season literally turns into a legal battle over the stigma of the non-earning husband.

There is a new hand on the wheel: **Sriraam Eragam** takes over directing duties from Arun Kothapally, working off the world built by creators **Mahi V Raghav** (of *Yatra*) and Pradeep Advaitham. The handover is barely noticeable, which is the highest compliment you can pay a franchise transition — the flavour is intact, the rhythm familiar, the comfort undiminished. Early reviews have landed around a solid 3 out of 5: not reinventing the wheel, but never forgetting that its only job is to keep you laughing on a weeknight, and doing it well.

For NRI households, *Save the Tigers* occupies a specific and beloved niche. It is not the prestige drama you queue up to impress your film-snob friends. It is the show you put on after a long week, the one that sounds like home — the cadences, the in-jokes about in-laws, the very particular comedy of Indian marriage that no Hollywood sitcom can replicate. That it now streams in multiple languages on JioHotstar means the half-Telugu, fully-confused second generation can finally follow along without a running translation from a parent on the sofa.

Is the fourth episode a touch flabbier than the riotous opening stretch? The franchise has historically dipped in its middle before recovering, and Season 3 is unlikely to break that pattern. But you do not come to *Save the Tigers* for narrative perfection. You come for three hapless men, one cosmically exasperated god, and the comforting reminder that somewhere out there, every husband thinks he has it the worst. Pour a chai, gather the family, and let Lord Indra sort out your weekend. Marriage, it turns out, is a problem big enough for the heavens.
